submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires retrospectively on the token that opens or continues a locally incomplete construction: a word-initial subword fragment that must still be completed (h+iked, N+airobi, am+oxicillin, j+', can+'t, light+-years), an open paren/bracket or markup/whitespace boundary that must be closed (range(, zeros((, O(, body><h1, indent space), or a short slot-projecting function word (a, and, is, not, did/do, because). Strength is highest for fragments and parens in a strongly projecting left context (pronoun verb-slot, enumeration slot, code call-head), weak (~0.1-0.4) for generic function words, and ~0 on construction-completing content words (walked, Paris, positive, guilty), on sentence punctuation, and on default high-frequency function words (the, of, to, in, on, are).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our route crossed three continents before the autumn ended, and none of us packed properly for any of them. We began in Lisbon, where the trams climb hills too steep for bicycles, and spent a whole week eating custard tarts near the harbor while gulls circled the fishing boats. From there we flew to Cairo, and the heat rose off the stones of the old mosques in visible waves that made the air shimmer at noon. My sister kept a diary of every single meal, rating each one out of ten with elaborate notes, and my father collected ticket stubs from every train we boarded along the way. The night train south rocked us to sleep with its rhythm, and we woke to palm trees and a river the color of hammered copper under a white sky. After Egypt we doubled back through Rome, where the rain turned the cobbles black and the museums stayed open late for the festival weekend with long lines at every door. A street musician played the same three songs outside our window each morning, and we never learned his name though we hummed along by the third day. Then came the long eastern leg, with layovers in Doha and Mumbai, running for gates and sleeping upright in plastic chairs beside departure boards we could barely read. My mother befriended a spice merchant who pressed packets of cardamom into her hands and refused payment with a smile. By the time we reached Kenya the whole family smelled of airplanes and strong tea, and our shoes were worn thin from cobbles and sand alike. The safari bus left Nairobi at dawn, rattling past markets piled high with mangoes and bright cloth, while our guide pointed out egrets standing in the roadside ditches. The booking agent had listed our remaining stops as Tokyo, Berlin, Nairobi and Lima on the printed itinerary, which made us laugh, since we had already visited half of them by accident.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout burying the Nairobi-style enumeration fragment deep in a travel narrative far from any example wording.
